title: Why Ships Aren't Rushing Through the Strait of Hormuz Yet
summary: Imagine a giant traffic jam at sea—over 250 oil tankers and 330 cargo ships are stuck inside the Persian Gulf, too scared to move. That's what's happening at the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway where about one-fifth of the world's oil usually passes through. President Trump announced on Sunday that the strait was 'open' after a deal with Iran, but experts say there are three big reasons ships aren't rushing out yet. First, security. Since February, Iran has fired on ships trying to cross without permission. The U.S. also blocked Iranian ports and even shot missiles at some ships. Even though Trump said the U.S. blockade would be removed, it's still in place until the deal is signed. Second, mines. Iran threatened to put floating mines in the water, and officials have warned about suspicious objects. Clearing mines could take months. Third, tolls? Actually, the third reason is fear. Ship captains remember April, when Iran said the strait was open, then closed it again the next day—forcing 33 ships to turn around while some were shot at. So now, nobody wants to go first. 'What we've been seeing is still very much a wait-and-see mentality,' said one expert. 'No-one really wants to be the first to take that risk.' Some brave companies might try soon, but for now, the world's oil is stuck in a floating parking lot.
why_it_matters: This situation could affect how much your family pays for gas, because oil delays might raise prices around the world.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow passage between Iran and Oman, connecting the Persian Gulf to the open sea. About one-fifth of the world’s oil travels through it on huge tankers.
President Donald Trump (the U.S. leader since 2025) said the strait was open, but ships still stayed because of past dangers. Iran has used floating mines and fired at ships before.
When so many tankers stop moving, the price of oil around the world can go up, making gas more expensive for everyone.
Article_Structure: WHO: Oil tankers, cargo ships, President Trump, Iran, ship captains
WHAT: Ships are stuck in the Persian Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz, too scared to pass even after Trump said it was open
WHERE: Strait of Hormuz, Persian Gulf
WHY: Three reasons are keeping ships still—security problems from Iran, floating mines in the water, and fear that the strait might suddenly close again

perspectives.description: They are scared to risk their ships and crews. Even if the U.S. says the path is safe, they remember how quickly things changed before and don't want to be the first to test it.
President Trump wants to show the strait is open for business and that a deal with Iran has worked. The U.S. aims to keep oil flowing smoothly.
Iran controls the strait and can threaten to close it or place mines. This gives them power over other countries that need the oil passing through.
